plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 15.2.12
plan.contextChunk: This figure is part of a worked example that evaluates the line integral of F = cos(x) i + sin(x) j along two different oriented curves. The figure contains two panels (a) and (b), each showing the same vector field F drawn over a green-shaded background with the note Vectors not to scale. Panel (a): the oriented curve C is a short vertical red line segment at x = -pi/2, directed downards from y = 2 to y = 1. Panel (b): the oriented curve C is a parabolic arc from (-1, 1) to (2, 4), directed first down, then upward and to the right. The figure shows the two distinct integration paths for parts (a) and (b) of the example, making visible how each curve's geometry and alignment relative to the field vectors determines the computed line integral. Note that the two parts of the image are differently scaled.

interactionPlan.concept: The line integral ∫_C F·dr accumulates the component of the vector field F = cos(x) i + sin(x) j that lies along the direction of travel, so its value depends on how the oriented curve is aligned with the field, not merely on its endpoints or length.
elements: Two stacked panels labeled (a) and (b), each a pale green shaded rectangle containing a vector field plot
Italic title above panel (a): 'Vectors not to scale'
Panel (a): x-axis with arrowhead and label x, y-axis with arrowhead and label y
Panel (a): tick labels 1 and 2 on the y-axis, tick label -π/2 on the x-axis (stacked fraction form)
Panel (a): grid of small black arrows representing F = cos(x) i + sin(x) j, all drawn at equal length (normalized), rotating direction with x
Panel (a): red vertical segment C at x = -π/2 from (-π/2, 2) down to (-π/2, 1), with red filled dot endpoints and a translucent red arrowhead midway pointing downward, label C beside it
Panel (b): x-axis with tick labels -2, -1, 1, 2, 3 and y-axis with tick labels 1, 2, 3, 4
Panel (b): same normalized arrow field on the green background, spanning roughly x ∈ [-2.3, 3.2], y ∈ [-0.6, 4.6]

Panel (b): red parabolic arc y = x² from (-1, 1) to (2, 4), with red filled dot endpoints and two translucent red arrowheads showing orientation (down-left branch then up-right branch), label C near the upper end
Panel captions '(a)' and '(b)' below each frame
Readout panel (added for the demo): current parameter t, position (x, y), field vector F at the point, unit tangent T, dot product F·T, and running value of ∫_C F·dr
Moving marker: a hollow red point on C with a blue field-vector arrow and a green tangent-vector arrow drawn from it, plus a shaded projection showing the component of F along T
Small inset accumulation plot of F·T ds versus t whose signed area equals the line integral

interactions.teaches: That the same field gives very different integrals along different oriented curves: the short vertical segment rides almost perpendicular/antiparallel to the field, while the long parabola sweeps through many field orientations.
interactions.label: Curve C

interactions.teaches: That reshaping the path — moving its endpoints through the field — continuously changes the accumulated integral, revealing which stretches of the curve contribute positively and which negatively.
interactions.teachesNote: Drag the red endpoint dots; the curve (segment or parabola through the endpoints) and the live integral update together.

interactions.teaches: That the integral is built pointwise: at each t the learner sees F, the unit tangent T, and their dot product, and watches the running total grow or shrink accordingly.
interactions.label: Parameter t along C

interactions.teaches: That the line integral is a continuous accumulation of F·T ds as the point traverses C in its given orientation.
interactions.label: Traverse C and accumulate

interactions.teaches: That only the projection of F onto the tangent direction matters — the perpendicular part of F contributes nothing to the line integral.
interactions.label: Show F·T decomposition

demo_steps.title: The field alone
demo_steps.narration: The green panel shows F = cos(x) i + sin(x) j, drawn with all arrows the same length so only direction is meaningful. Notice the direction depends only on x: vertical columns of identical arrows, swinging from downward near x = -π/2 to rightward near x = 0.

demo_steps.title: Curve (a): straight down at x = -π/2
demo_steps.narration: The oriented curve C runs from (-π/2, 2) down to (-π/2, 1). Along this whole column the field points straight down — exactly with the direction of travel — so every contribution is positive.

demo_steps.title: Step along (a)
demo_steps.narration: Slide t: the field vector never changes, the tangent never changes, so F·T is constant and the running integral grows linearly to its final value.

demo_steps.title: Curve (b): the parabola y = x²
demo_steps.narration: Now the path runs from (-1, 1) down through the origin and up to (2, 4). The tangent swings from pointing down-right to steeply up-right while the field rotates with x, so F·T changes sign along the way.

demo_steps.title: Accumulate along (b)
demo_steps.narration: Play the sweep: watch the running total dip where F opposes the tangent and climb where they align. The inset shows the signed area that is the integral.

demo_steps.title: Compare the two paths
demo_steps.narration: Side by side, the short vertical segment and the long curved arc give different values in the same field. Then drag the endpoints of either curve and watch the number move — the integral is a property of the oriented path, not just its endpoints.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A line integral measures alignment: at every point only the component of F along the direction you are moving counts, so a path that runs with the field accumulates positively, a path that runs against it subtracts, and a path perpendicular to it contributes nothing at all.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two stacked framed panels on a pale mint-green background, each with black axes drawn with arrowheads extending slightly past the green rectangle. Field arrows are short, uniform-length black arrows on a regular lattice; their direction is cos(x) i + sin(x) j, so arrows are constant along vertical lines and rotate as x increases — straight down near x = -π/2, rightward near x = 0, up-right for x > 0, up-left for x < -π. Italic serif note 'Vectors not to scale' centered above panel (a). Panel (a) is zoomed in: y ticks at 1 and 2, a single x tick labeled -π/2 as a stacked fraction; the curve C is a thick red vertical segment from (-π/2, 2) to (-π/2, 1) with solid red endpoint dots and a semi-transparent red triangular arrowhead at its midpoint pointing downward, italic label C to its right. Panel (b) is zoomed out: x ticks -2, -1, 1, 2, 3 and y ticks 1-4; the curve C is a thick red parabola y = x² from (-1, 1) to (2, 4) with red endpoint dots and two translucent red arrowheads indicating travel down-left-to-origin then up-to-right, italic label C near the upper right end. Panel captions '(a)' and '(b)' in italic parentheses below each frame. For the interactive layer, add a hollow red moving marker on C with a blue arrow for F, a green arrow for the unit tangent T, a dashed projection of F onto T when the decomposition toggle is on, and a compact readout box (t, x, y, F, T, F·T, running ∫_C F·dr) plus a small inset curve of F·T ds vs t with shaded signed area.

discrepancies: Orientation of curve C in panel (a) is reversed: the source draws the translucent arrowhead pointing UP (path from (-π/2, 1) to (-π/2, 2)), while the generated segment runs downward from (-π/2, 2) to (-π/2, 1); the narration then reports a positive integral of 1 where the source's depicted orientation would give -1.

The '−π/2' x-axis label is typeset as separate glyphs plus a hand-drawn fraction bar; in the render the minus, π, bar and 2 sit nearly on top of one another and of the axis, producing a cramped/illegible stack compared with the clean stacked fraction in the source.

The source's two-panel stacked composition is replaced by a single panel at default (panel (b) only reachable via dropdown); acceptable as a toggle, but the default view is noticeably less complete than the source at a glance, and the 'both' layout places panels side-by-side rather than stacked.

Field arrows are rendered with thinner strokes and slightly smaller heads than the bold hand-drawn arrows of the source, so the vector field reads fainter; the source's arrows also have visibly larger arrowheads relative to shaft length.

The 'Show F·T decomposition' checkbox label is broken across several lines in the control panel ('Show / F / . / T / decomposition') with the checkbox detached above it, making the control hard to parse.
evaluation.notes: A faithful and well-built recreation of the vector-field figure with rich, genuinely pedagogical interactions (panel toggle, parameter slider, animated traversal, F·T decomposition, draggable endpoints, 6-step demo), but the panel-(a) curve is traversed in the opposite direction from the source (flipping the sign of the integral relative to the textbook example) and the −π/2 fraction label is badly typeset and collides with itself.

feedback.rationale: The interaction concept and decomposition are sound; the issues are concrete implementation defects—reversed curve orientation, collided −π/2 fraction typesetting, wrapped checkbox label, and thin arrow strokes—that belong to the generator.

discrepancies: Orientation of curve C in panel (a) is reversed: the source shows the translucent arrowhead pointing UP (travel from the lower dot toward the upper dot, against the downward field), while the generated figure traverses DOWN and its narration asserts F·T = +1 everywhere — this flips the sign of the integral relative to the textbook figure.
The title 'Vectors not to scale' collides with the y-axis arrow and the italic 'y' axis label at the top of the panel; in the source the title sits well clear above the axis.

Composition/scale: the panel occupies only the upper-left ~45% of the 640×560 canvas, leaving a large empty white band on the right and bottom in the default (step-0) state, whereas the source fills its frame.
Axis tick labels (1, 2) and the stacked −π/2 fraction are rendered noticeably smaller relative to the panel than in the source and partly blend into the black field arrows.

Only panel (a) is shown by default (panel (b) and the side-by-side view are behind the 'Curve C' selector / demo steps) — acceptable as a toggle, but the source presents both panels stacked as a single composite figure.
evaluation.notes: Faithful reproduction of the F = cos x i + sin x j field panel with correct green background, normalised arrow lattice, red oriented curve and ticks, backed by an unusually rich and functional interaction set (6-step player, curve selector, t slider, animated accumulation, F·T decomposition, draggable endpoints); main weaknesses are the reversed orientation of C in panel (a) versus the source, a title/y-axis label collision, and a large amount of unused canvas in the default view.

Move the 'Vectors not to scale' title above the panel top (or shift the panel down) and reposition the 'y' label so neither overlaps the y-axis arrowhead.

Enlarge the panel (or centre it) in the single-panel modes so the artwork fills the canvas instead of leaving ~half the frame blank in the step-0 state; scale tick/axis label font sizes with the panel.
Add a light white halo or larger font to the numeric tick labels so they read clearly over the dense black arrow lattice.

plan.concept: The line integral ∫_C F·dr accumulates the component of the vector field F = cos(x) i + sin(x) j that lies along the direction of travel, so its value depends on how the oriented curve is aligned with the field, not merely on its endpoints or length.
elements: Two stacked panels labeled (a) and (b), each a pale green shaded rectangle containing a vector field plot
Italic title above panel (a): 'Vectors not to scale'
Panel (a): x-axis with arrowhead and label x, y-axis with arrowhead and label y
Panel (a): tick labels 1 and 2 on the y-axis, tick label -π/2 on the x-axis (stacked fraction form)

Panel (a): red vertical segment C at x = -π/2 from (-π/2, 2) down to (-π/2, 1), with red filled dot endpoints and a translucent red arrowhead midway pointing downward, label C beside it
Panel (b): x-axis with tick labels -2, -1, 1, 2, 3 and y-axis with tick labels 1, 2, 3, 4

Panel (b): red parabolic arc y = x² from (-1, 1) to (2, 4), with red filled dot endpoints and two translucent red arrowheads showing orientation (down-left branch then up-right branch), label C near the upper end
Panel captions '(a)' and '(b)' below each frame

interactions.teaches: That the same field gives very different integrals along different oriented curves: the short vertical segment rides almost perpendicular/antiparallel to the field, while the long parabola sweeps through many field orientations.
interactions.label: Curve C

interactions.teaches: That reshaping the path — moving its endpoints through the field — continuously changes the accumulated integral, revealing which stretches of the curve contribute positively and which negatively.
interactions.teachesNote: Drag the red endpoint dots; the curve (segment or parabola through the endpoints) and the live integral update together.

interactions.teaches: That the integral is built pointwise: at each t the learner sees F, the unit tangent T, and their dot product, and watches the running total grow or shrink accordingly.
interactions.label: Parameter t along C

interactions.teaches: That the line integral is a continuous accumulation of F·T ds as the point traverses C in its given orientation.
interactions.label: Traverse C and accumulate

interactions.teaches: That only the projection of F onto the tangent direction matters — the perpendicular part of F contributes nothing to the line integral.
interactions.label: Show F·T decomposition

demo_steps.title: The field alone
demo_steps.narration: The green panel shows F = cos(x) i + sin(x) j, drawn with all arrows the same length so only direction is meaningful. Notice the direction depends only on x: vertical columns of identical arrows, swinging from downward near x = -π/2 to rightward near x = 0.

demo_steps.title: Curve (a): straight down at x = -π/2
demo_steps.narration: The oriented curve C runs from (-π/2, 2) down to (-π/2, 1). Along this whole column the field points straight down — exactly with the direction of travel — so every contribution is positive.

demo_steps.title: Step along (a)
demo_steps.narration: Slide t: the field vector never changes, the tangent never changes, so F·T is constant and the running integral grows linearly to its final value.

demo_steps.title: Curve (b): the parabola y = x²
demo_steps.narration: Now the path runs from (-1, 1) down through the origin and up to (2, 4). The tangent swings from pointing down-right to steeply up-right while the field rotates with x, so F·T changes sign along the way.

demo_steps.title: Accumulate along (b)
demo_steps.narration: Play the sweep: watch the running total dip where F opposes the tangent and climb where they align. The inset shows the signed area that is the integral.

demo_steps.title: Compare the two paths
demo_steps.narration: Side by side, the short vertical segment and the long curved arc give different values in the same field. Then drag the endpoints of either curve and watch the number move — the integral is a property of the oriented path, not just its endpoints.

plan.keyInsight: A line integral measures alignment: at every point only the component of F along the direction you are moving counts, so a path that runs with the field accumulates positively, a path that runs against it subtracts, and a path perpendicular to it contributes nothing at all.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Two stacked framed panels on a pale mint-green background, each with black axes drawn with arrowheads extending slightly past the green rectangle. Field arrows are short, uniform-length black arrows on a regular lattice; their direction is cos(x) i + sin(x) j, so arrows are constant along vertical lines and rotate as x increases — straight down near x = -π/2, rightward near x = 0, up-right for x > 0, up-left for x < -π. Italic serif note 'Vectors not to scale' centered above panel (a). Panel (a) is zoomed in: y ticks at 1 and 2, a single x tick labeled -π/2 as a stacked fraction; the curve C is a thick red vertical segment from (-π/2, 2) to (-π/2, 1) with solid red endpoint dots and a semi-transparent red triangular arrowhead at its midpoint pointing downward, italic label C to its right. Panel (b) is zoomed out: x ticks -2, -1, 1, 2, 3 and y ticks 1-4; the curve C is a thick red parabola y = x² from (-1, 1) to (2, 4) with red endpoint dots and two translucent red arrowheads indicating travel down-left-to-origin then up-to-right, italic label C near the upper right end. Panel captions '(a)' and '(b)' in italic parentheses below each frame. For the interactive layer, add a hollow red moving marker on C with a blue arrow for F, a green arrow for the unit tangent T, a dashed projection of F onto T when the decomposition toggle is on, and a compact readout box (t, x, y, F, T, F·T, running ∫_C F·dr) plus a small inset curve of F·T ds vs t with shaded signed area.

discrepancies: The stacked −π/2 label is drawn on top of an opaque white rectangle that reads as an added callout box punched into the green field panel; the source has the fraction sitting directly on the background with no box.

The 'C' label in panel (a) sits very close to the red segment (roughly one glyph-width away) and is partly crowded by the field arrows, whereas in the source it stands clearly in open space to the right of the segment.

Panel (a) is rendered nearly square and much wider than the source's tall, narrow portrait panel, so the column structure of the field looks stretched horizontally and the segment occupies a smaller fraction of the frame than in the original.

The field lattice is sampled at cell centres and is noticeably denser/larger-headed than the source, and the arrows run right across the axis lines and tick numerals, giving a busier look than the original where the axes read clearly through the lattice.
Default view shows only panel (a); panel (b) exists behind the 'Curve C' dropdown (correct per the toggle), but the side-by-side stacked composition of the source is never the default.
evaluation.notes: A faithful and conceptually correct reproduction of the (a) panel of the cos(x)i + sin(x)j field with its upward-oriented segment, backed by a rich and correctly-wired interaction set (step player, curve selector, t-slider, sweep animation, F·T decomposition, draggable endpoints); main weaknesses are cosmetic — an opaque white box behind the −π/2 fraction, a crowded 'C' label, and a panel aspect/arrow density that departs from the source's tall, airier layout.
action_items: Replace the opaque white rectangle behind the −π/2 fraction with a text halo (paint-order stroke) so the label blends into the green panel like the source.
Move the 'C' label further from the red segment (and away from the nearest field arrows) in panel (a) so it reads as an annotation in open space, matching the source placement.

Constrain panel (a) to a taller, narrower aspect closer to the source (roughly 3:4) and reduce field arrow head size / stroke weight slightly so axis lines and tick numerals read clearly through the lattice.
Consider making the default step show panels (a) and (b) stacked (or at least offer a stacked layout option) so the step-0 state reads as a drop-in replacement for the two-panel source image.
